scenes.narration: How fast is light, really? And why does it matter for everything you see?
In a vacuum, light travels at exactly two hundred ninety nine million, seven hundred ninety two thousand, four hundred fifty eight metres every second.

data.label: Exact, because the metre is defined from it

scenes.narration: People tried to measure it for centuries. Roemer made the first estimate in sixteen seventy six, Fizeau timed it on Earth in eighteen forty nine, and by nineteen eighty three the metre itself was defined by light.

events.label: Roemer's first estimate, from Jupiter's moons
Fizeau times it on Earth with a toothed wheel
The metre is defined by the speed of light

scenes.narration: It sounds fast, but space is big. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, forty three minutes to reach Jupiter, and over four hours to reach Neptune.

data.title: Light travel time from the Sun

scenes.narration: So when you look at the Sun, you are seeing it as it was eight minutes ago.

data.caption: Every glance at the sky is a look back in time

scenes.narration: Compare that with sound. Light is roughly eight hundred seventy thousand times faster than sound travelling through air.

left.label: Sound in air
left.note: A thunderclap arrives long after the flash.

scenes.narration: Why can nothing outrun it? Anything with mass would need unlimited energy to reach that speed. Light has no rest mass, so it has no choice. And space and time adjust so that everyone measures the same speed.

data.title: Why nothing outruns light
items: Anything with mass would need unlimited energy
Light has no rest mass, so it must travel at that speed
Space and time adjust so every observer measures the same speed

scenes.narration: That is the speed limit of the universe. Follow for the next one.

data.title: The speed limit of the universe
